short: A short-term loan at checkout that lets you buy something now and pay for it in a few instalments, often interest-free if paid on time.
kid: You take a toy home today and promise to bring the coins in three small parts over the next few weeks. If you forget a part, you have to bring a little extra.
detail: Buy now pay later (BNPL) splits a purchase into a few instalments, typically four payments over about six weeks, or offers a short credit line at checkout. The merchant usually pays the provider a fee, often higher than a card fee, because BNPL raises sales and basket sizes; the shopper pays no interest if every instalment is on time but may face late fees. Global players include Klarna and Afterpay. In India, BNPL is treated as lending: after the RBI barred loading credit lines onto prepaid wallets and cards in 2022, providers must lend through a bank or NBFC under the digital lending rules, and repayments are reported to credit bureaus. The common confusion is that 'interest-free' means risk-free. A missed instalment can hurt your credit score, and juggling several plans at once makes it easy to overspend.
example: Say you buy a ₹12,000 phone on a pay-in-4 plan: ₹3,000 today and ₹3,000 every two weeks, so it is fully paid after six weeks. The shop, say ABC Electronics, pays the BNPL provider a 4% fee of ₹480 and receives ₹11,520.
formula: Instalment = Purchase price / Number of instalments

short: A bank-like service that exists only as a phone app, with no branches; in India it usually runs on top of a licensed partner bank.
kid: Imagine a piggy bank that lives inside a phone. There is no building to visit; you just tap to save and spend.
detail: A neobank offers accounts, cards, payments and money-management tools entirely through an app, with no branches, aiming for lower costs and a better experience than traditional banks. Some abroad hold full banking licences, such as Monzo and Starling in the UK. In India the RBI does not license neobanks as a separate category, as of 2025, so neobank apps partner with licensed banks: the bank holds the deposits and carries the regulatory duty, while the app owns the customer relationship and earns from card fees, loan referrals and investment distribution. Because payments earn little, profits usually depend on selling credit, and many neobanks struggle to break even. The common confusion: an Indian neobank app is not itself a bank. Your money's safety, including deposit insurance, depends on the partner bank where it actually sits.
example: Say a neobank, XYZ Money, has 10 lakh users and earns ₹40 a month per user from card fees and loan referrals, while serving each user costs ₹50 a month. It loses ₹10 per user, or ₹1 crore a month, which is why neobanks push hard to sell loans.

short: A system where you can let approved apps securely see your bank data or start payments from your account, through standard digital connections.
kid: Your piggy bank keeps a list of every coin. Open banking means you can say, 'Yes, my teacher may look at that list,' and only for as long as you allow.
detail: Open banking is a framework in which banks share a customer's account data, or allow payments to be started from the account, with authorised third parties through secure application programming interfaces (APIs), but only with the customer's explicit consent. The UK's Open Banking programme and the EU's PSD2 rules, both live from 2018, are the best-known models. It powers faster loan approvals, budgeting and comparison apps, and account-to-account payments that bypass card networks. Open finance extends the idea to investments, pensions, insurance and tax data. India took its own route: licensed account aggregators carry encrypted, consented data between institutions, while UPI already handles payment initiation. The common confusion is that open banking makes your data public. It is consent-based, purpose-limited sharing, designed to replace risky habits such as handing your banking password to an app.
example: Say Riya applies for a ₹2 lakh personal loan from a lender, say ABC Finance. With her consent, the lender reads 12 months of statements in seconds, sees an average monthly salary of ₹60,000 and existing EMIs of ₹12,000, and works out that EMIs already take 20% of her income, all without her uploading a single PDF.

short: An RBI-licensed go-between that moves your financial data from one institution to another, only after your digital consent, without reading it itself.
kid: An account aggregator is like a trusted postman. He carries a sealed letter about your piggy bank from one grown-up to another, but only when you say yes, and he never opens it.
detail: An account aggregator (AA) is a special type of NBFC licensed by the RBI under directions issued in 2016. It moves data from Financial Information Providers, such as banks, mutual fund registrars, insurers, pension funds and the GST system, to Financial Information Users, such as lenders and wealth managers. You approve a consent request that specifies what data, for what purpose and for how long, and you can revoke it. The data travels encrypted, and the AA is 'data blind': it cannot read or store it. The network went live in September 2021. Sahamati is the industry alliance that coordinates participants; it is neither a regulator nor an AA. It matters because lenders can verify income and cash flows in minutes, helping MSMEs and thin-file borrowers. The common confusion: an AA is not a credit bureau and does not score you; it only carries data you allow.
example: Say a shop owner applies for a ₹5 lakh working-capital loan. Through an AA she lets the lender, say ABC Finance, see six months of bank statements and GST returns for seven days. The lender sees sales averaging ₹4 lakh a month, or ₹24 lakh over six months, and approves the loan the same day.

short: Financial services such as loans, payments or insurance offered inside a non-financial app or website, supplied in the background by a licensed provider.
kid: When you buy a bicycle, the toy shop lets you pay a little each week right at the counter. A helper from another shop is quietly making that possible in the back.
detail: Embedded finance puts a financial product at the moment a customer needs it: EMI options at an online checkout, trip insurance on a travel site, working-capital loans inside a seller app or accounting software. Banking as a Service (BaaS) is the supply side, where licensed banks and NBFCs expose accounts, cards, payments and lending through APIs so other brands can build on them. Typically the brand owns the customer, a tech firm runs the plumbing and the regulated entity holds the licence, the balance sheet and the compliance duty. Distribution costs fall and conversion rises. The risk is that responsibility blurs along the chain: the 2024 collapse of US middleware firm Synapse left more than 100,000 customers unable to reach funds held at partner banks, and regulators have since sharpened scrutiny of partner-bank models. The common confusion: the brand you see is usually not the lender or insurer.
example: Say an online furniture store, ABC Living, offers a six-month plan at checkout funded by a partner NBFC. A ₹60,000 sofa becomes six payments of ₹10,000, and the store pays the NBFC a 5% fee of ₹3,000 so the buyer pays no interest.

short: Lending where the whole journey, from application and checks to payout and repayment, happens online through apps or websites.
kid: Instead of going to a big building to borrow coins, you ask on a phone and the coins arrive in minutes. You still have to give them all back.
detail: Digital lending covers personal loans, small-ticket credit, BNPL and MSME loans where application, credit checks, disbursal and collection all happen online. In India, the RBI's digital lending rules, first issued in September 2022 and consolidated into directions in 2025, set the framework. Only a regulated entity, such as a bank or NBFC, can lend; an app or fintech that sources, services or collects loans for it is a lending service provider (LSP). Money must flow directly between the lender's and borrower's bank accounts, the borrower must get a key fact statement showing the all-in annual percentage rate, a cooling-off period allows exit without penalty, and apps cannot freely harvest phone data. The rules followed a wave of illegal loan apps that used harassment to recover dues. The common confusion: the app's brand is often not the lender, so check the lender named in the key fact statement.
example: Say a student borrows ₹20,000 on an app for three months and repays ₹7,000 a month, with a ₹500 processing fee deducted upfront. She receives ₹19,500 but repays ₹21,000, so the total cost of credit is ₹1,500, which the key fact statement must show before she signs.

short: A fintech partner's promise to cover a bank's or non-bank lender's first losses on loans the fintech brought in, up to a fixed cap.
kid: Your friend says, 'Lend your crayons to these kids, and if any break, I will replace the first few myself.' That promise makes you happier to lend.
detail: In fintech-bank partnerships, a lending service provider sources borrowers while a bank or NBFC books the loans. To show it has skin in the game, the fintech promises to compensate the lender for defaults up to a fixed share of the portfolio. Long called a first loss default guarantee (FLDG), it was formally permitted by the RBI in June 2023 as a default loss guarantee (DLG). Under the rules as of 2025, cover is capped at 5% of the portfolio, must be backed by cash, a fixed deposit or a bank guarantee, and must be invoked within 120 days of a loan becoming overdue. The lender must still do its own underwriting and recognise bad loans as usual. For investors, a DLG is a hidden credit exposure of the fintech. The common confusion: a DLG does not make loans risk-free; losses above the cap fall entirely on the lender.
example: Say ABC Bank disburses ₹100 crore of loans sourced by a fintech that gives a 5% DLG backed by a ₹5 crore fixed deposit. If defaults total ₹3 crore, the bank recovers all ₹3 crore from the guarantee. If defaults reach ₹8 crore, the bank recovers only ₹5 crore and bears the remaining ₹3 crore itself.
formula: Lender's loss = max(0, Defaults - DLG cap), where DLG cap = DLG % × Portfolio amount

aliases: Public Tech Platform for Frictionless Credit
hl: public tech platform for frictionless credit
short: An RBI-built digital platform that lets lenders pull a borrower's data, such as land records and bank statements, from many sources at once, with consent.
kid: Before a grown-up lends you coins, they want to see your report card, your chores list and your piggy bank. This is one big window where they can see all of them at once, if you allow it.
detail: The Unified Lending Interface (ULI) is a platform built by the Reserve Bank Innovation Hub, piloted from August 2023 as the Public Tech Platform for Frictionless Credit and renamed ULI in August 2024, when the RBI Governor described JAM, UPI and ULI as a new trinity of India's digital infrastructure. It connects lenders through standard APIs to many data sources, such as state land records, satellite crop data, dairy cooperative records, GST and account aggregator data and identity checks, all with the borrower's consent. The aim is to cut the time and cost of small loans to farmers and MSMEs, where paperwork is heavy and ticket sizes small; it is being extended to more lenders as of 2025. The common confusion: ULI is not a lender, a loan marketplace or a credit bureau. It is plumbing that fetches verified data so banks and NBFCs can decide faster.
example: Say a dairy farmer seeks a ₹1.6 lakh Kisan Credit Card loan. Through ULI the bank fetches his land record, his bank statement and his milk-cooperative payments of ₹20,000 a month, or ₹2.4 lakh a year, in one go, and sanctions the loan within a day instead of after several branch visits.

short: Judging whether someone will repay a loan using non-traditional data, such as bill payments, bank cash flows or GST records, not only past borrowing.
kid: A girl has never borrowed crayons before, so nobody knows if she gives things back. But she always returns her library books on time, so her friends decide to trust her.
detail: Traditional credit scores rely on a borrowing track record, so new-to-credit (NTC) people, such as students, first-time earners, gig workers and small shopkeepers, are often invisible to lenders. Alternative credit scoring fills the gap with other signals: rent, electricity and phone bill payments, bank account cash flows shared through account aggregators, UPI transaction patterns, GST filings and online sales, usually fed into machine-learning models. For MSMEs this is often called cash-flow based lending. It widens access to credit and can price risk more finely. The risks are opaque models, hidden bias against certain groups and privacy intrusion; India's digital lending rules bar apps from accessing contact lists, files and call logs. The common confusion: alternative data supplements credit bureau data rather than replacing it, and being new to credit is not the same as being a bad borrower. It simply means the lender knows less.
example: Say applicants A and B both have no loan history. A's statements show a steady ₹40,000 monthly salary and 12 on-time phone bill payments in a row; B's show irregular income and three bounced payments. A lender using alternative data might offer A a loan with a ₹4,000 EMI, just 10% of her income, and decline B, though both have the same blank bureau report.

short: Online platforms that connect people wanting to lend money directly with individuals or small businesses wanting to borrow, without a bank in between.
kid: Instead of putting your coins in the big piggy bank, you lend a few to a friend down the street who promises to give them back with a little extra. A helper writes down who lent what.
detail: Peer-to-peer (P2P) lending platforms list borrowers, assess them and handle collections, while individual lenders choose whom to fund; the platform earns fees from both sides. In India every such platform must be registered with the RBI as an NBFC-P2P. Under the rules as of 2025, a lender can put at most ₹50 lakh across all P2P platforms, a lender's exposure to any one borrower across platforms is capped at ₹50,000, and a borrower can owe at most ₹10 lakh across platforms. Money moves through escrow accounts, and the platform cannot guarantee returns or absorb losses. In 2024 the RBI tightened the rules to stop products sold with fixed returns and anytime withdrawal, which made P2P look like a deposit. The common confusion: P2P lending is not a fixed deposit. The lender bears the full credit risk with no deposit insurance, and it is unrelated to person-to-person UPI payments.
example: Say Arjun lends ₹1 lakh on a P2P platform, ₹10,000 each to 10 borrowers at 14% a year, repayable in one lump sum after a year. If nine repay ₹11,400 each and one defaults completely, he gets back ₹1,02,600, a gain of ₹2,600 or 2.6%, not the 14% advertised.
formula: Net return = (Total repaid - Amount lent - Fees) / Amount lent

short: Verifying a customer's identity online, for example through an Aadhaar OTP, fingerprint or a live video call, instead of paper forms and branch visits.
kid: Before you join a club, someone checks that you really are you. This check happens on a phone, by looking at your face or sending a secret number, so you do not have to go there.
detail: Know Your Customer (KYC) is the identity and address verification that banks, NBFCs, brokers and insurers must do under anti-money-laundering law, in India the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. eKYC does it digitally. Aadhaar eKYC lets UIDAI confirm a person through an OTP or biometrics and share their name, address and photo with an authorised entity. Video KYC, formally the Video-based Customer Identification Process (V-CIP), allowed by the RBI since January 2020, has a trained official verify the customer on a live video call with liveness checks and geotagging. The Central KYC Records Registry lets a completed KYC be reused. It slashed onboarding costs and powered the demat account boom. The common confusion: not all eKYC is equal. Accounts opened through OTP-based eKYC without video or in-person checks carry balance limits under the rules as of 2025 and must be upgraded to full KYC within a year.
example: Say ABC Bank spends ₹400 per customer on paper KYC and ₹40 on video KYC. Onboarding 1 lakh new customers would cost ₹4 crore on paper but ₹40 lakh digitally, a saving of ₹3.6 crore.

short: A digital form of a country's official money, issued directly by its central bank, just like banknotes but in electronic form.
kid: Imagine the grown-ups who make the real paper notes also made special notes that live only inside a phone. They are just as real as the notes in your piggy bank.
detail: A central bank digital currency (CBDC) is a direct liability of the central bank, like banknotes, whereas money in a bank account is a claim on a commercial bank and a stablecoin is a claim on a private issuer. Retail CBDC is meant for everyday payments by the public; wholesale CBDC is for banks and financial institutions settling large transactions. Most designs are two-tier: the central bank issues and banks distribute. Live examples include the Bahamas' Sand Dollar and Nigeria's eNaira, while China's e-CNY and India's digital rupee run large pilots; the US went the other way in 2025, when an executive order barred federal agencies from promoting a CBDC. Supporters cite cheaper payments and public money in a cashless world; critics worry about privacy and deposits fleeing banks in a panic. The common confusion: a CBDC is not cryptocurrency. It is centralised, legal tender and as stable as cash.
example: Say a family holds ₹50,000: ₹10,000 in banknotes, ₹30,000 in a bank deposit and ₹10,000 in retail CBDC. The ₹20,000 in notes and CBDC is a direct claim on the central bank, while the ₹30,000 deposit is a claim on the commercial bank.

short: India's central bank digital currency: rupees issued by the RBI in digital form, held in a phone wallet and as valid as cash.
kid: The digital rupee is like a coin from the official money-maker that lives in your phone instead of your pocket. You can hand it to a shopkeeper with a tap.
detail: The digital rupee (e₹) is the RBI's central bank digital currency, made possible when the Finance Act 2022 amended the RBI Act so that bank notes can be issued in digital form. The RBI launched a wholesale pilot (e₹-W) on 1 November 2022 for settling government-securities trades between banks, and a retail pilot (e₹-R) on 1 December 2022 for people and merchants. Retail e₹ is token-based and held in e₹ wallet apps offered by participating banks; users can pay one another or scan merchants' UPI QR codes. Like cash, it earns no interest. The RBI has also tested offline payments and programmable money, which can be restricted to specific uses such as subsidies. The common confusion: e₹ is neither a crypto token nor a UPI balance. UPI moves bank deposits, while e₹ is RBI money itself. Usage remains small next to UPI as of 2025.
example: Say Meera loads ₹2,000 from her bank account into her e₹ wallet and pays a vegetable seller ₹150 by scanning his UPI QR code. Her wallet now holds ₹1,850 in digital rupees, which, like ₹1,850 in notes, is a claim on the RBI rather than on her bank.

short: Shared, government-backed digital systems for identity, payments and data sharing that anyone, including private firms, can build services on.
kid: Roads are built once for everyone, and then any bus or bicycle can use them. This is like roads, but for phones, so many apps can travel on the same paths.
detail: Digital public infrastructure (DPI) means open, interoperable digital building blocks, usually identity, payments and data exchange, provided as public goods on which both government and private firms build services. India's version, often called India Stack, layers Aadhaar digital identity (over 130 crore numbers issued by 2025), eKYC and eSign, UPI for payments, DigiLocker for documents and account aggregators for consented data sharing, with newer rails such as ONDC and ULI. The G20 under India's 2023 presidency endorsed a framework for DPI, and other countries run comparable rails, such as Brazil's Pix payments system. For finance, DPI slashes the cost of onboarding, payments and underwriting, which supported Jan Dhan financial inclusion and the rise of fintechs and discount brokers. The common confusion: DPI is not a government app or a state monopoly on services. The state builds the roads; private players run the vehicles on them.
example: Say a lender spends ₹3,000 to process a ₹30,000 loan the old way, 10% of the loan, but only ₹300 using Aadhaar eKYC, account aggregator data and UPI disbursal, just 1%. Small loans that were not worth making become viable.

short: A government-backed open network that lets shoppers on any participating app buy from sellers listed on any other participating app.
kid: Usually you can only buy sweets from the shop whose door you walk into. This is like a big street where you can see every shop's sweets from any door.
detail: The Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) is a not-for-profit company backed by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT); it began pilots in 2022. It is a set of open protocols, not an app: buyer apps, seller apps and logistics providers plug into the network, so a seller listed once can be discovered by shoppers on any participating app. The aim is to reduce dependence on a few large marketplaces, lower commissions for small merchants and kirana stores. Food and grocery orders surged in 2023 on the back of discounts and slowed when incentives were cut, and the network has since added financial products such as loans, insurance and mutual funds. For investors, it could reshape platform commission rates and give lenders data on small sellers. The common confusion: ONDC itself neither sells nor delivers anything, and it is not the government procurement portal GeM.
example: Say a bakery, ABC Bakes, sells a ₹500 cake. On a closed marketplace charging a 25% commission it keeps ₹375; through ONDC, where the buyer app, seller app and delivery partner together take, say, 10%, it keeps ₹450, or ₹75 more per cake.

short: Software that helps financial firms follow regulations more cheaply and reliably, for example by automating identity checks, fraud monitoring and reports to regulators.
kid: A school has lots of rules. This is like a helpful robot that reminds everyone of the rules and quietly checks that nobody is breaking them.
detail: Regtech covers tools that automate compliance: onboarding and KYC, anti-money-laundering transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, fraud detection, trade surveillance, regulatory reporting and tracking rule changes. It grew after the 2008 crisis, when new rules sent compliance headcounts and costs soaring, and it now leans heavily on data analytics and AI. When regulators use the same ideas to supervise, it is called suptech; examples include the RBI Innovation Hub's MuleHunter.AI tool for spotting mule accounts and SEBI's data-driven market surveillance. It matters because compliance failures are expensive: in 2024 TD Bank pleaded guilty in the US to anti-money-laundering failures and agreed to pay about $3 billion. The common confusion: buying a regtech tool does not transfer legal responsibility. The regulated bank or broker remains accountable for every alert its software misses.
example: Say ABC Bank has 50 analysts, each reviewing 40 suspicious-transaction alerts a day, or 2,000 alerts in all. A regtech tool that correctly screens out 70% as false alarms leaves 600 alerts, so the same team can study each remaining case far more closely.

short: Technology firms and tools that change how insurance is sold, priced, issued and claimed, usually through apps, data and automation.
kid: If your toy breaks, a kind helper has promised to help buy a new one. This lets you get that promise on a phone, and get help quickly when something breaks.
detail: Insurtech covers online insurance marketplaces and brokers, digital-first insurers such as Acko and Go Digit, micro-insurance embedded at checkout, usage-based motor cover priced on how much or how well you drive, parametric policies that pay automatically when a trigger such as heavy rainfall or a flight delay is met, and AI tools for underwriting and claims. In India, insurers and intermediaries are regulated by IRDAI, which allowed pay-as-you-drive motor add-ons in 2022 and has backed Bima Sugam, an online insurance marketplace designed to work like public digital infrastructure. It matters because insurance coverage in India remains low relative to the size of its economy, and cheaper distribution and faster claims could widen it. The common confusion: many insurtechs are only distributors. The risk, and your claim, sits with the licensed insurer whose name is on the policy.
example: Say a flight-delay cover costs ₹99 and pays ₹2,000 automatically if a flight is more than three hours late. If 1,000 travellers buy it and 30 of them face such a delay, the insurer collects ₹99,000 in premiums and pays out ₹60,000.

short: Technology that helps people invest and manage money, such as investing apps, online brokers, robo-advisors and portfolio-tracking tools.
kid: This is like a phone game that helps you grow your savings jar. It shows how much is inside and helps you choose where to put your coins.
detail: Wealthtech covers discount brokers, direct mutual fund platforms, robo-advisors, portfolio trackers that pull holdings through account aggregators or consolidated account statements, and apps for fractional or thematic investing. In India such apps, alongside low-cost brokerage, helped demat accounts jump from about 4 crore in March 2020 to over 19 crore by early 2025. Business models vary: brokerage fees, subscriptions, distribution commissions, advisory fees and interest on margin funding. SEBI regulates each role separately, so an app may be a stockbroker, a mutual fund distributor, an investment adviser or several at once. Easy, gamified access can also encourage overtrading: a 2024 SEBI study found that about 93% of individual futures and options traders lost money over three years. The common confusion: an investment app is usually a broker or distributor, not your adviser, and its suggestions may not be regulated advice.
example: Say an investor's fund holdings average ₹6 lakh and her wealthtech app moves her from a regular plan with a 1.5% expense ratio to the direct plan of the same fund at 0.5%. She saves 1% a year, or ₹6,000 annually in costs.

short: An app or online service that builds and manages an investment portfolio for you automatically, using algorithms based on your goals and comfort with risk.
kid: This is like a robot helper that sorts your coins into different jars for later. It checks the jars often and moves coins around so they stay in the right mix.
detail: A robo-advisor asks about your goals, time horizon and risk tolerance, uses an algorithm to recommend an asset allocation, usually built from low-cost index funds or ETFs, invests the money and rebalances automatically, sometimes adding tax-loss harvesting. Betterment and Wealthfront popularised the model in the US from around 2010, and large firms such as Vanguard and Charles Schwab launched their own. Fees are often a fraction of what traditional human advisers charge. In India, a platform giving automated advice must be registered with SEBI as an investment adviser and is held to the same suitability and disclosure standards as a human adviser. It matters because it brings disciplined, diversified investing to small savers and pushes industry fees lower. The common confusion: 'robo' does not mean smarter forecasts. Most robo-advisors simply apply standard portfolio theory and periodic rebalancing.
example: Say a robo-advisor targets 60% equity and 40% debt on ₹1 lakh. After a rally, equity grows to ₹75,000 while debt stays at ₹40,000, a total of ₹1,15,000 with equity at about 65%. To restore 60:40 it sells ₹6,000 of equity and buys ₹6,000 of debt, leaving ₹69,000 and ₹46,000.
formula: Amount to sell = Current value of asset - Target weight × Total portfolio value (a negative result means buy)

short: A controlled test where regulators let firms try new financial products on real customers, at small scale, with some rules relaxed, for a limited time.
kid: Before building a big sandcastle on the beach, you practise in a small sandbox in the garden. If it falls, nobody gets hurt and you learn what to fix.
detail: A regulatory sandbox lets firms test innovative financial products with real customers under a regulator's watch, with a limited user base, transaction caps, a fixed time window, customer safeguards and some rules eased. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority launched the first in 2016. The RBI's sandbox framework, introduced in 2019, runs cohorts on themes such as retail payments, cross-border payments, MSME lending and fraud prevention, alongside theme-neutral cohorts; SEBI, IRDAI and IFSCA run their own, and an inter-operable sandbox handles products that span regulators. At the end, the regulator reviews the results and decides whether the product can scale and whether rules need changing. It matters because regulators learn about new technology before writing rules, and start-ups get a path to market. The common confusion: entry into a sandbox is not a licence or an endorsement. The firm still needs full authorisation to launch.
example: Say a fintech, ABC Pay, is admitted to a sandbox to test offline payments with up to 5,000 users, a cap of ₹2,000 per transaction, for six months. If every user made one maximum payment on the same day, the total would be ₹1 crore, an exposure the regulator can size in advance.

short: A single phone app that bundles many services, such as chat, payments, shopping, travel, loans and investing, so users rarely need other apps.
kid: This is like one big toy box that holds your crayons, your ball, your puzzles and your piggy bank. You open one box and find everything.
detail: A super app starts with a service people use many times a day, such as chat, payments or rides, then adds shopping, travel, bill payments, credit, insurance and investing behind one login, using shared data to cross-sell. The model took off in Asia with China's WeChat and Alipay and Southeast Asia's Grab and Gojek. In India, Paytm, PhonePe and Tata Neu have pursued versions of it. Because ordinary UPI payments carry no merchant fee under the rules as of 2025, Indian super apps rely on lending, insurance and investment distribution to make money. Regulators worry about concentration and risk spillover: the RBI's 2024 business restrictions on Paytm Payments Bank showed how problems in one entity can hit an entire app's ecosystem. The common confusion: a super app is not one licensed institution. Each financial service usually sits with a different regulated company or partner.
example: Say a super app, XYZ, has 5 crore monthly users. If 1% take a loan through it and the app earns ₹1,000 in sourcing fees per loan, that is 5 lakh loans and ₹50 crore in fees, far more than free UPI payments bring in.

short: A person whose bank account is used, knowingly or not, to receive and pass on stolen money so criminals can hide where it came from.
kid: A stranger hands you a bag and asks you to carry it to someone else for a sweet. If the bag was stolen, you have helped hide it, even though you did not steal it.
detail: Fraudsters behind phishing, fake investment schemes and digital arrest scams move victims' money within minutes through layers of bank accounts before withdrawing cash or converting it into crypto, a classic money-laundering step. Those accounts often belong to students, job seekers or daily-wage workers who sell or rent out their account, debit card, UPI ID or SIM for a small fee, sometimes unknowingly. Banks and the RBI treat mule accounts as a top fraud risk: the RBI Innovation Hub announced MuleHunter.AI in December 2024 to flag likely mule accounts using machine learning, and accounts reported through the national cybercrime helpline 1930 can be frozen. It matters because fraud losses and weak KYC bring penalties and reputational damage for banks. The common confusion: 'I only lent my account' is no defence. Mule account holders can face frozen accounts and prosecution even if they never met the scammer.
example: Say a scammer tricks a victim into sending ₹9 lakh, split across three mule accounts at ₹3 lakh each. Each mule forwards ₹2.9 lakh to the next layer and keeps ₹10,000, so ₹8.7 lakh moves on within hours while the three mules earn ₹30,000 together, and each now risks a frozen account and prosecution.

short: A wallet, card or voucher you load with money in advance and spend from later, such as a mobile wallet, metro card or gift card.
kid: You give the canteen some coins at the start of the week, and they give you a card. Each time you buy a snack, the card remembers how much is left.
detail: Prepaid payment instruments (PPIs) are regulated by the RBI's Master Directions on PPIs. Closed-system PPIs, usable only with the issuer, such as a store's own gift card, are outside RBI authorisation. Other PPIs, such as mobile wallets, prepaid cards, transit cards and meal cards, can be issued by banks or RBI-authorised non-banks, which must keep customers' money in an escrow account with a bank. Under the rules as of 2025, a small PPI with minimal KYC can hold at most ₹10,000, a full-KYC PPI up to ₹2 lakh, and a gift PPI up to ₹10,000 without reloading; full-KYC PPIs must work with UPI and card networks. In 2022 the RBI barred loading PPIs from credit lines, ending card-based BNPL on prepaid cards. The common confusion: a PPI balance is not a bank deposit. It earns no interest and has no deposit insurance.
example: Say Ravi loads ₹5,000 into a full-KYC wallet and spends ₹1,200 on groceries and ₹800 on metro rides. His balance is ₹3,000; it earns no interest, and the wallet company must hold matching money in an escrow account at a bank.

short: A sticker with a radio chip on a vehicle's windscreen that lets Indian toll plazas deduct the toll automatically from a linked account or wallet.
kid: This is a magic sticker on the car's window. When the car rolls up to the gate, the gate reads the sticker, takes the coins from the family's jar and opens by itself.
detail: FASTag is a radio-frequency identification (RFID) sticker read by scanners at toll plazas; the payment runs on NPCI's National Electronic Toll Collection (NETC) system, and tags are issued by banks and linked to a prepaid wallet or bank account. It became mandatory for four-wheelers on national highways in February 2021, with vehicles lacking a valid tag charged a higher toll. Rules on KYC, one tag per vehicle and blocking of low-balance or misused tags have tightened since, and an annual pass for private cars was introduced in August 2025. Authorities are also testing barrier-free tolling based on satellite positioning and number-plate cameras. It matters because it cut waiting times and cash leakage, and monthly FASTag collections are watched as a high-frequency indicator of road traffic and economic activity. The common confusion: FASTag is a payment method, not a toll exemption; the toll is still charged, just automatically.
example: Say a car crosses a toll plaza charging ₹120 per trip 20 times in a month. FASTag deducts ₹2,400 from the linked wallet, so a ₹3,000 recharge leaves ₹600 at month-end.

short: Paying through UPI apps with borrowed money, from a RuPay credit card or a bank-approved credit line, instead of from your savings account.
kid: Normally you pay the ice-cream man with coins from your own jar. Here, a grown-up pays for you right away, and you give the coins back later.
detail: Until 2022, UPI could only pull money from savings and current accounts. In September 2022 RuPay credit cards could be linked to UPI apps, and from September 2023 banks could also link pre-sanctioned credit lines to UPI. These payments mainly go to merchants rather than to friends. Under the rules as of 2025, ordinary UPI payments carry no merchant fee, but RuPay credit card payments on UPI carry a merchant discount rate, with small merchants exempt on payments up to ₹2,000, giving card issuers a revenue model; Visa and Mastercard credit cards cannot be linked to UPI. It matters because credit cards can now work at millions of small shops that accept only UPI QR codes, which could grow card usage and lending. The common confusion: it is still borrowing. Card interest, fees and credit score effects apply exactly as with a swiped card.
example: Say Neha pays a café ₹450 by scanning its UPI QR code with her linked RuPay credit card. Her savings account is untouched; the ₹450 is added to her card bill, which rises from ₹18,000 to ₹18,450, and she pays no interest if she clears the full bill by the due date.

short: A phone or video-call scam where fraudsters pose as police or other officials, falsely accuse you of a crime and pressure you into transferring money.
kid: A stranger calls pretending to be a police officer and says you are in big trouble unless you hand over your piggy bank. Real police never ask for your piggy bank on a phone call.
detail: Scammers call, often by video, posing as police, the CBI, the Enforcement Directorate, customs or a courier firm, and claim that a parcel with drugs or a bank account used for money laundering is linked to the victim. They keep the victim on camera for hours or days, in a so-called digital arrest, isolated and frightened, until savings are moved to a 'safe' or 'verification' account. Indian law has no such thing as a digital arrest; agencies do not interrogate or collect money over video calls, a warning the Prime Minister repeated in October 2024. The money then flows through mule accounts. The wider family of cyber and UPI fraud includes fake collect requests, QR codes, phishing links and trading-app scams. The common confusion: you never need to enter a UPI PIN to receive money. Report fraud on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in to improve the chance that funds are frozen.
example: Say a scammer pushes a retired teacher to move ₹40 lakh in two transfers of ₹25 lakh and ₹15 lakh. If she reports it on 1930 within the hour and police freeze the ₹15 lakh still sitting in a mule account, that part may be recovered, but the ₹25 lakh already moved on may be lost.
